e.etymology: A phonetic spelling of Arthur from 19th-century American records, matching the word author. Arthur is a Celtic name often linked with a word for bear.
e.note: Identical to the word author, so it will be read as the word and not as a form of Arthur.

e.etymology: A pet form of names beginning with Oz- or Os-, such as Oscar, Oswald and Ozella, used by both men and women around 1900.
A phonetic spelling of Emma as it was said in parts of the rural United States, where a final a became er. Emma comes from a Germanic word for whole or universal.
The English adjective vernal, of the spring, from Latin vernalis. It was used as a first name beside Vernon and Verne in the early 1900s.
A feminine form of Shelby with the ending of Melba, used mostly in the American South in the 1930s and 1940s.
Wanda with the prefix To-, a 1960s American pattern. Towanda is also a town in Pennsylvania, and the name is shouted as a battle cry in the 1991 film Fried Green Tomatoes.
A spelling of Tamika, an American name of the late 1960s, perhaps taken from the Japanese name Tamiko, which the 1962 film A Girl Named Tamiko brought to notice.
The Scandinavian form of German Werner, an old Germanic name built from a word for watchful or guarding and heri, army.
A phonetic three-syllable spelling of Henry, from the Germanic words heim, home, and ric, ruler.
namesakes: Henery Hawk (the tiny chicken hawk in Looney Tunes cartoons)

e.etymology: The English word, used as a pet name and then entered as a given name for both boys and girls in the American South around 1900.
e.note: Reads as the ordinary word toy, which invites jokes.

assoc.t: toy, the everyday word for a plaything

e.etymology: A spelling of Carol, which began as a short form of Caroline, a feminine form of Charles, from a Germanic word for a free man.
A pet form of names beginning with Os-, such as Oscar and Osborne, used by both men and women around 1900.
A spelling of Farrell, an Irish surname from O Fearghail, descendant of Fearghal, a name meaning man of valor.
An elaboration of Flora with the diminutive ending -etta, from Latin flos, flower.
A pet form of names such as Ona, Leona and Iona, entered as a given name in the late 1800s.
An English surname from the town of Ewell in Surrey, whose name comes from Old English aewell, the source of a river.
An American coinage of the 1970s that adds the prefix Ta- to Kisha, a form of Keisha.
A spelling of Gordon, a Scottish surname from a place in Berwickshire, thought to be Brittonic for a spacious fort.
A form of Karen or the French Carine written with the -een ending of Maureen and Doreen.
The English color word and surname. As a 19th-century Southern first name it came from the surname, sometimes in honor of the Revolutionary War general Nathanael Greene.
A short form in the family of Delphia and Delphine, names that go back to Delphi, the Greek site of Apollo's oracle.
A misspelling of Benjamin, from Hebrew Binyamin, son of the right hand, the youngest son of Jacob in the Book of Genesis.
A Welsh name, either from glyn, valley, or a form of Glenys, from glan, pure or holy. The Welsh actress Glynis Johns made it known in America.
namesakes: Glynis Johns (actress, Mrs. Banks in Mary Poppins)

e.etymology: The English name of the spice, from Greek kinnamomon. Its brief run as a girl's name around 1969 followed the character Cinnamon Carter on the TV series Mission: Impossible.
From the Germanic words hild, battle, and beraht, bright.
A spelling of Darryl, from the English surname Darrell, brought by Normans who came from Airelle in Calvados, France.
The German and Dutch form of Theresa, a name first recorded in Spain. Its origin is uncertain; it is often linked with Greek therizein, to harvest, or the island of Therasia.
The short form of Herbert, from the Germanic words hari, army, and beraht, bright.
namesakes: Herb Alpert (trumpeter and leader of the Tijuana Brass)
Herb Brooks (coach of the 1980 Miracle on Ice hockey team)

assoc.t: herb, a seasoning plant; also slang for marijuana
